title: Buttermilk biscuits
skill: Cutting in cold fat, folding for layers

notes.2: Makes 12 biscuits. Use two sheet pans and swap their racks halfway through baking.
notes.0.5: Makes 3 biscuits. Pat the dough into a smaller rectangle.

move.title: Cold butter, flaky layers
move.body: Keep the butter cold and in little pieces, then fold the dough over itself. In the hot oven the butter melts and lets off steam, and the steam puffs the layers apart.

why.title: Why the butter has to be cold
why.body: Cold butter stays in solid little pieces in the flour. In a hot oven those pieces melt fast and turn to steam, which pushes the dough up into flaky pockets. Warm butter just mixes in, and the biscuits come out flat.

why.title: Don't overmix
why.body: Stirring flour with liquid builds gluten, which makes dough stretchy and tough. Mix just until it comes together, even if it still looks lumpy and rough.

why.title: Why fold the dough
why.body: Each fold stacks the butter pieces into layers. Three folds give you lots of thin layers you can peel apart once it's baked.

why.title: Cut straight down
why.body: Twisting the cutter pinches the edges shut, so the layers can't rise. Press straight down and lift straight up.

wrong.sign: The dough is too sticky to handle
wrong.fix: Dust it and your hands with a little flour. Don't knead more flour in.

wrong.sign: The butter is getting soft and greasy
wrong.fix: Slide the whole bowl into the freezer for 10 minutes.
The butter was too warm, or the cutter got twisted. Next time, freeze the butter longer and cut straight down.

quiz.explain: Cold butter pieces melt and steam in the hot oven, puffing the layers apart. Baking powder helps the rise, but the layers come from the butter.

steps.text: Put a rack in the middle of the oven and heat it to 450°F. Line the sheet pan with parchment.
Put the butter in the freezer.
steps.tip: Measure everything else while it chills.

steps.text: Whisk the flour, baking powder, baking soda, salt, and sugar together in the big bowl.
Grate the frozen butter on the large holes of the box grater, straight into the flour. Toss with the fork so every shred is coated.
steps.tip: Hold the butter by its wrapper so your warm hands don't melt it.

steps.text: Pour in the buttermilk. Stir with the fork just until there's no dry flour left. It should look lumpy and rough, not smooth. That's right, so stop stirring.
steps.tip: Don't taste the raw dough. Raw flour can make you sick.

steps.text: Dust the counter with flour and tip the dough out. Pat it into a rectangle about 1 inch thick, about as thick as two of your fingers stacked. Fold it in thirds like a letter, turn it a quarter turn, and pat it out again. Do this 3 times.
Pat the dough two fingers thick one last time. Press the cutter straight down, lift it straight up, and set each biscuit on the pan with the sides touching.
steps.tip: Gently press the scraps together to cut the last ones. They won't be quite as tall.

steps.text: Brush the tops with melted butter if you like. Bake until tall and golden brown.
steps.look: Golden brown on top, and the bottoms are browned too.

steps.text: Use oven mitts to take out the pan. Move the biscuits to the rack and let them cool for a few minutes.

preheat.text: Heat the oven to 450°F. Line the sheet pan with parchment.

dry.text: Spoon and level the flour into the big bowl. Whisk in the baking powder, baking soda, salt, and sugar.
dry.tip: Spoon the flour into the cup, then scrape it flat. Don't scoop.

wet.text: Pour in the buttermilk. Stir with the fork just until no dry flour is left.
wet.tip: Don't taste the raw dough. Raw flour can make you sick.

fold.text: Fold it in thirds like a letter. Pat it out again. Do this 3 times.

cut.text: Press the cutter straight down and lift straight up. Set the biscuits on the pan, sides touching.

bake.text: Bake until tall and golden brown.
bake.look: Tall, and golden brown on top and bottom.

cool.text: With an adult and oven mitts, take out the pan. Move the biscuits to the rack to cool.
cool.look: Flaky layers when you pull one apart.

add.text: Cut the cold butter into small cubes with the butter knife. Put them on the plate in the freezer.
add.tip: Measure everything else while it chills.

add.text: Add the cold butter. Press it into the flour with the fork until the pieces are the size of peas.
add.look: Crumbs with pea-sized bits of butter.
add.tip: Work fast. Warm butter melts into the flour.

add.text: Tip the dough onto a floured counter. Pat it into a rectangle about 1 inch thick.
add.look: About as thick as two fingers stacked.

move.title: Cut in the cold butter
move.body: Biscuits get their flaky layers from little pieces of cold butter. This week you'll cut cold butter into flour with a fork until the pieces are the size of peas, stir in buttermilk, and fold the dough to stack the layers.

wrong.sign: The dough is too sticky to handle
wrong.fix: Dust it and your hands with a little flour. Don't knead more flour in.

wrong.sign: The butter is getting soft and greasy
wrong.fix: Slide the whole bowl into the freezer for 10 minutes.
The butter was too warm, or the cutter got twisted. Next time, freeze the butter longer and cut straight down.

wrong.sign: The butter turned into a paste
wrong.fix: It got too warm. Put the bowl in the freezer for 10 minutes, then keep going.

quiz.explain: Cold butter pieces melt and steam in the hot oven, puffing the layers apart. Baking powder helps the rise, but the layers come from the butter.

quiz.q: How big should the butter pieces be?
quiz.explain: Each piece makes a flaky pocket.

quiz.q: Why cut the biscuits straight down?
choices: Twisting pinches the edges shut, so they can't rise
quiz.explain: Press straight down, lift straight up.

add.title: Pea-sized pieces
add.body: Pressing cold butter into flour with a fork breaks it into small pieces coated in flour. Each piece melts into steam in the oven and leaves a flaky pocket. Pieces the size of peas are just right.
